newsitem.title: TURKEY: Inflation fears keep Turkish bond yields high.
newsitem.headline: Inflation fears keep Turkish bond yields high.

text.p: Turkish treasury bill and bond rates are likely to remain around 115-125 percent in the coming months because of higher inflation expectations and a persistent cash squeeze, bankers said.

Yields began rising from the 100 percent level on July 14 after a 30 percent jump in petroleum prices, and the rise was further fuelled by Economy Minister Gunes Taner's remarks that inflation could climb to 100 percent by end-year.

"Under current conditions I see no reason for interest rates to go down. We expect bond yields to move around 115-125 percent levels in the coming months as the market expects higher inflation," the securities manager at a private bank said.

"Although inflation expectations have a major impact on the interest rate trend, a persistent cash shortage and the government's domestic borrowing policy will determine rates in the future," he added.
The treasury has not auctioned t-bills since July 15. It said it had no need for borrowing while it is preparing to launch new borrowing instruments.

At its July 15 auction after the formation of a new government under Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz, the treasury sold 280 trillion lira worth of 11-month t-bills at an average yield of 104 percent (excluding witholding tax).
But t-bill yields have jumped since then amid expectations of rising inflation. T-bill and bond yields topped 120 percent last week but later settled at around 117-118 percent.
"The trend of bond yields depends on the treasury's borrowing policies and July inflation figures due on August 4," a private bank treasurer said.
Markets were relaxed despite Taner's comment last week that inflation could rise to 100 percent in 1997.

Sentiment was helped further by an agreement signed on Wednesday by Treasury chief Mahfi Egilmez and central bank governor Gazi Ercel pledging cooperation in fighting chronic inflation. The two restated their aim of keeping annual inflation below 90 percent.
Inflation is currently at about 80 percent and Turkish markets expect it to be around 90 percent for 1997 as a whole.
The jump in bill and bond yields prompted Turkish banks to raise their lira deposit rates last week.
One-month rates rose to 70-76 percent from 65-70, three months to 80-82 percent from 75-76, six-month to 85-90 from 80-82 percent and one-year rates to 95-100 percent from 90.

The central bank raised its short-term money market lending rates by one to two points to 74 percent last week, while average overnight repos were held at 80 percent because of a continuing cash shortage. -- Istanbul newsroom +90-212-275 0875
